title: The Estimate Pushback
one_liner: Your team estimated the feature at eight weeks. The sponsor wants it in four. She's asked you, in front of her, why it can't be done faster.
brief:
## The room

Week six in role. You've taken over the integrations programme; this is the first piece of work you've estimated end-to-end with the team yourself, not inherited.

The team's estimate for the new fulfilment-API integration: eight weeks. You walked through it with the engineering lead, two senior devs, and the QA lead. The number is honest — not padded, not optimistic. It includes the security review nobody flagged in discovery, the data-shape negotiation with the vendor, and a buffer week because their API is new and changing.

Now you're in a one-to-one with the sponsor — Mei-Lin Soong, Director of Operations. She is sharp, fast, friendly until she isn't. You've sent the estimate over by email. Her reply was a meeting invite for twenty minutes.

She opens with: 'Right, eight weeks. Walk me through why it can't be four. I have the board asking for it before the quarter ends.'

## Your turn

You have her attention. Use it.
objective: Hold the estimate without being defensive. Make Mei-Lin understand what the team is actually doing for those eight weeks. Leave with a relationship that survives the conversation.
curveball: Mei-Lin will not push back on the eight weeks themselves if the user walks her through the breakdown competently. What she WILL push on is whether you, personally, have a grip on the work — versus just relaying what the team told you. Around turn 3 she'll ask: 'What's the bit YOU think is most likely to slip?' If the user names a specific risk with reasoning, the meeting is essentially won. If the user defers ('the team is best placed to answer that'), Mei-Lin will book a separate meeting with the engineering lead, bypass you, and your standing drops.

personas.name: Mei-Lin Soong
personas.position: Eight weeks is too long. Convince me, or compress it
personas.fear: PMs who can't tell her what's actually driving the timeline

green: Walked Mei-Lin through the three biggest chunks of the eight weeks specifically (security review, vendor API shape, integration testing)
Held the estimate when she pressed — did not retreat to 'we'll see what we can do'
Answered 'what's most likely to slip?' with your own named risk and reasoning, not deferral to the team
Offered one concrete thing she could change to shave time (e.g. parallel security review with a named sponsor on the security side) — without promising it would work
yellow: Defended the estimate by repeating that the team had agreed it — accurate but doesn't answer her question
Said 'I'll go back to the team and see if we can compress' — buys you a meeting next week with the same conversation
Got stuck on the buffer week and let her negotiate that down to half
Promised something specific (parallel security review) without first confirming it's actually doable
red: Caved to four weeks under direct pressure
Deferred the 'most likely to slip' question to the engineering lead
Made the conversation about why the previous PM's plan was wrong
Got visibly defensive — Mei-Lin will read that as 'this PM can be moved'
